content: Each year, approximately 16 million cases of whooping cough (pertussis) occur globally, with the majority of cases arising in low-income countries. A significant portion of the illness in both children and adults is attributed to the effects of the characteristic paroxysmal cough. Various treatments have been proposed to alleviate this cough, including corticosteroids, beta2-adrenergic agonists, pertussis-specific immunoglobulin, antihistamines, and potentially leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs). The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of interventions aimed at reducing the severity of paroxysmal cough in children and adults with whooping cough. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, CINAHL, and LILACS, up to January 30, 2014. They also reviewed ongoing trials through Current Controlled Trials. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that investigated interventions other than antibiotics and vaccines for suppressing the cough associated with whooping cough. Two independent reviewers selected trials, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the studies. The primary outcome of interest was the frequency of paroxysmal coughing episodes. Secondary outcomes included the frequency of vomiting, whooping, and cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin), the development of serious complications, mortality from any cause, medication side effects, hospital admissions, and the duration of hospital stays. A total of 12 trials were included, with sample sizes ranging from 9 to 135 participants, involving a total of 578 individuals. Most of the studies were conducted in high-income countries. Ten trials focused on children (448 participants), while two trials included adolescents and adults (130 participants). Only three trials were deemed to have high methodological quality, evaluating diphenhydramine, pertussis immunoglobulin, and montelukast. The results of the included studies did not demonstrate statistically significant benefits for any of the interventions. Six trials, involving 196 participants, provided sufficient data for detailed analysis. Diphenhydramine did not significantly alter the frequency of coughing episodes, with a mean difference (MD) of 1.9 coughing spells per 24 hours (95% confidence interval [CI]: -4.7 to 8.5; 49 participants in one trial). One trial on pertussis immunoglobulin suggested a possible reduction of 3.1 whoops per 24 hours (95% CI: -6.2 to 0.02; 47 participants), but it did not affect the length of hospital stay (MD: -0.7 days; 95% CI: -3.8 to 2.4; 46 participants). Dexamethasone did not show a clear reduction in hospital stay duration (MD: -3.5 days; 95% CI: -15.3 to 8.4; 11 participants in one trial). Salbutamol also did not reduce the frequency of coughing paroxysms per day (MD: -0.2; 95% CI: -4.1 to 3.7; 42 participants in two trials). Adverse events were reported in only one trial comparing pertussis immunoglobulin to placebo (47 participants). In the treatment group, 4.3% of participants experienced a rash, while in the placebo group, 5.3% experienced side effects such as loose stools, pain, and swelling at the injection site. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of interventions for managing the cough associated with whooping cough. Further high-quality trials are necessary to evaluate the potential benefits of antitussive treatments in patients with this condition.
